problem_data.story:
The neural interface lab in Dalebrook Town hummed with the quiet efficiency of expensive equipment. I nearly tripped over the kid before I saw her in the dim corridor outside the observation room.

Her wheelchair was positioned where it usually was during evening hours, near the large window overlooking the research campus courtyard. But tonight something was different. Priya wasn't watching the courtyard gardens as she typically did, tracking the movements of people approaching the entrance with that intense focus that had first caught my attention months ago. Instead, she sat with her head tilted back, staring at the ceiling-mounted neural activity display that showed real-time brain scans of research subjects.

The girl wasn't observing the data streams tonight as she usually did. She was lying back in her chair with her face turned upward, her eyes following patterns that seemed to exist only in her mind, so absorbed that she didn't notice me until I spoke.

"Everything okay, Priya?" I asked.

She said, "Yes, Dr. Wolfe," without shifting her gaze from the display.

For a moment I experienced an odd sensation of déjà vu, as if I'd lived through this exact scene before. The feeling puzzled me until I remembered a similar encounter three months earlier, when Dr. Nathan Hamilton and I had first brought our mobile research unit to the Dalebrook Neurological Institute. I'd nearly stumbled over Priya's wheelchair that time too, but she hadn't been studying neural patterns then. She'd been watching the entrance, waiting.

"What are you looking at up there, Priya?" I asked.

She didn't move, and her voice had that distant quality I'd learned to recognize.

"I'm reorganizing some connections," she said softly.

I gave up and continued to my shared office without pressing further. How do you talk to a child prodigy like that?

Nathan wasn't in, but for once I didn't worry about him. I was trying to recall what had seemed so familiar about finding Priya's wheelchair out of place. I retrieved a coffee from our small machine—I think better with something warm in my hands—and by the time I'd finished it, I had my answer.

This scenario was familiar because it had happened before, about three months back when Nathan and I first established our research presence at Dalebrook. I'd nearly stumbled over Priya that time too, but she wasn't reorganizing neural connections then. She was just staring ahead, waiting.

She'd been sitting in her wheelchair near the window, gazing out at the courtyard entrance. She was practically holding her breath, as if expecting someone important to arrive, so absorbed that she didn't notice me until I spoke. With her slight frame, serious expression, and unnaturally still dark eyes, she reminded me of those unsettling child actors in psychological thrillers. Except there was nothing theatrical about her intensity. Maybe that's why I spoke, because she looked so desperately focused.

"Something wrong, kid?" I asked.

She didn't startle or look up. Her accent placed her as second-generation immigrant, probably South Asian based on her name and features.

"Someone's supposed to come back," she said, keeping her eyes on the entrance. "I need to be here when they arrive."

I might have asked who she was expecting, but just then the observation room door opened behind her and her mother took over.

I couldn't see Susan Stanley well because the lights were dimmed inside for the neural imaging equipment. But I could tell from her silhouette that she was tall and imposing. I could make out the glow of a tablet screen in her hands, and when she looked up—the blue light illuminating her face—I saw she was in her mid-thirties, professional-looking but with an edge of exhaustion that spoke of long hours and difficult decisions.

"This isn't your concern, Dr. Wolfe," she said. Her voice was educated, professional, but with an undercurrent of protective fierceness. "Please don't encourage Priya's fixations."

She was right about it being none of my business. I went on to the office I shared with Nathan Hamilton and left the two of them there together.

Our office was dark, which meant first that Nathan had probably gone to the faculty lounge as soon as I left that morning to run my experiments, and second that he'd probably gotten too caught up in philosophical debates to remember to come back. But I was wrong on at least one count, because when I switched on the light and set down my research notes, I saw Nathan asleep on the small couch we'd requisitioned.

He'd been drinking coffee, though. I could smell it on him when I shook him awake—strong, institutional coffee that spoke of long hours in the lounge discussing epistemology with anyone who would listen.

Nathan sat up and blinked against the fluorescent lights, a thin man in his fifties with graying temples, wire-rimmed glasses, and rumpled clothes that suggested he'd been sleeping in them. He was still wearing his lab coat, though at some point during the day he'd managed to shave. He'd even organized some papers; they sat in a neat stack on his desk with a half-written grant proposal on top.

"Wake up and help me write this progress report, Nathan," I said, holding him to his end of our research partnership. "I've collected three months of data and the ethics board wants documentation."

Nathan got up and stretched. He walked to my desk and poked at my notes.

"Cortical plasticity studies again," he complained. "Diego, I'm tired of measuring brain waves!"

"You don't get tenure by studying philosophy," I told him. And because I'd never been able to stay annoyed at him for long, I added, "But we have fresh coffee. Where's your mug?"

"I'm tired of coffee, too," Nathan said. "I need a real conversation about something meaningful."

I gestured at the air, making a show of it. "You've been having one already. Where?"

He grinned at me then with that self-aware, intellectually mischievous expression that transformed his face and made him different from every other burned-out academic I'd ever met.

"The bounty of human curiosity," he said, "is distributed impartially across disciplines and departments. I helped young Priya to the restroom this afternoon while her mother was conducting interviews, and my kindness was justly rewarded."

Sometimes it's hard to tell when Nathan is being serious. He's a trained philosopher—used to teach at some prestigious Eastern university, he'd mentioned once, and I never doubted it—and speaks like one when he chooses to. But Nathan's no deadbeat, though he's semi-obsessed with existential questions and lets me carry most of our research load, and he's perceptive enough to read my thoughts like a data stream.

"No, I didn't barge into her private files," he said. "Susan—Ms. Stanley—shared information with me voluntarily. Why else do you suppose I'd organize those papers?"

That was like Nathan. He hadn't violated research ethics though his curiosity was probably eating him alive. He'd organized grant proposals instead, making himself useful enough to warrant Susan sharing what she knew.

"Fair enough," I said and poured coffee for both of us while Nathan pulled up our data files.

He told me more about the Stanleys while we reviewed the research. Susan and Priya were permanent residents of Dalebrook. The girl—she was twelve—was a neurological anomaly who hadn't walked for over two years following a severe accident, and her mother was a research coordinator at the Institute studying rehabilitation techniques. There wasn't any Mr. Stanley. I guessed there never had been, which would explain Susan's protective intensity.

"Priya's quite attached to certain people," Nathan said, scrolling through data. "She forms intense bonds—intellectual connections, really. When someone captures her interest, she becomes almost obsessive about their presence, their schedule, when they'll return. Susan worries about it."

We were halfway through the data review when I remembered the girl at the window.

"Who is she expecting?" I asked. "She mentioned someone coming back."

Nathan's expression shifted slightly. "Priya had a mentor at one point. A neuroscientist who worked at the Bristol facility—brilliant woman, apparently, specialized in neural plasticity and consciousness studies. There was some kind of incident there, a research accident, around the same time Priya was hospitalized for her own injury."

"And this mentor left?"

"The Bristol facility had significant damage," Nathan said carefully. "Several researchers were affected. Susan hasn't given me all the details, but the program there was essentially terminated."

I thought of the girl sitting out there every evening in her wheelchair, watching the entrance. "That's a long time to keep expecting someone."

Nathan seemed to lose interest in the Stanleys then, so I let the subject drop. We worked through the evening and finished the progress report around midnight. When we shut down for the night, I figured we wouldn't be staying long at the Dalebrook Institute. It wasn't a very comfortable research environment.

I was wrong there. It wasn't comfortable, but we stayed.

I couldn't have explained at first why we remained, and if Nathan could, he didn't volunteer the information. Neither of us discussed it. We just continued our routine, a few months here and a few there, following grant funding across the country.

We'd arrived at the Dalebrook facility too late for the main consciousness studies funding cycle, so I focused on peripheral research instead. I worked on cortical mapping projects all the way from basic sensory processing to complex decision-making paradigms, not committing to any of the major research teams because I prefer mobility when I get restless. I chose independent neural plasticity studies mostly, because the publication potential is good there if you've got strong analytical skills and patience for data collection.

Neural mapping isn't the exciting frontier it seems to graduate students who flock to the field because the technology is cutting-edge. You work with sophisticated equipment, usually, scanning brain activity instead of direct observation, and you use multiple measurement modalities that capture activity at the cellular level where the real changes occur. There's no dramatic breakthrough moment, as the students discover quickly. A neural reorganization happens gradually, and the biggest challenge is documenting the incremental changes once you've identified a pattern.

Usually a researcher like me publishes findings through the Institute's channels or collaborates with some established team that wants additional data for their meta-analyses, and there's nearly always recognition—from a pool of competitive researchers at the beginning of every funding cycle—for the person documenting the most significant plasticity event. There's a knack to identifying meaningful patterns, and when the grants were running well I only worked a few days a week and spent the rest of my time in the office playing chess and drinking coffee with Nathan Hamilton.

Usually it was an ideal academic life, but somehow it wasn't enough at this place. We'd get moderately caffeinated and work up a promising debate about the nature of knowledge or the foundations of consciousness. Then, just when we'd gotten epistemology looking its most fascinating with our arguments, one or the other of us would glance out the window and see Priya Stanley in her wheelchair, positioned at the entrance, watching. She was always there, morning or evening, until her mother finished work and took her home.

Nathan developed a routine with the girl. He'd stop by her wheelchair each morning and afternoon, and she'd look up at him with that intense focus of hers. "Will you be here all day?" she'd ask him, or "When are you coming back?" and Nathan would tell her his schedule, patient as always.

"She tracks everyone's movements," Nathan explained to me once. "It's how she copes with uncertainty—knowing when people will return."

It wasn't right or natural for a child to wait like that for anything, and it troubled me. I even offered once to arrange for Priya to meet other mentors in the field, but Susan Stanley told me quickly to mind my own business. Nathan explained later that the girl didn't want another mentor because she had what he called an epistemological fixation.

"The person Priya's waiting for was more than just a teacher to her," Nathan said. "That relationship represented validation and possibility. With someone like that mentoring her, Priya felt intellectually validated, and she could envision possibilities beyond her physical limitations. If she accepted another mentor now, she'd be abandoning more than a person. She'd be abandoning everything that relationship represented, and then there wouldn't be any point in pursuing knowledge."

I could understand it when Nathan framed it that way. The mentor had spent considerable time with Priya, and the girl felt as intellectually secure with her as she would have with a tenured faculty advisor. Together, they'd been an ideal partnership.

The Stanleys grew accustomed to Nathan and me being around. Priya particularly attached herself to Nathan's schedule, asking after him whenever he stepped out. "Where's Dr. Hamilton going?" she'd ask me if Nathan left for the lounge. "He said he'd be back by three." Once I found her anxiously positioned where she could see both the courtyard entrance and the corridor to our office, as if monitoring two arrivals simultaneously.

That routine started every morning when Leonardo Simmons, the Institute's mail courier, rolled his cart through from the main building to deliver correspondence and packages. Leonardo would always make it a point to stop by the observation room window, and Priya would intercept him.

"Any news from Bristol?" she'd ask. "Anything about the consciousness research program there?"

Old Leonardo would pause with his cart and remove his cap, frowning while he pretended to consider.

Then he'd say, "Not today, Priya," or, "Heard some faculty transferred out, but no details."

Then he'd continue on, shaking his head. Later the maintenance staff would come around to service the equipment, and Priya would inquire about Bristol news too. Once a month the administration sent someone to conduct facility inspections, and they became part of Priya's routine as well.

It was hard on Susan. Sometimes the girl would have vivid dreams at night that someone was working in the old Bristol lab, and she'd wake Susan and beg her to make inquiries. When that happened, Nathan and I could hear Susan talking to her through the thin walls of the residential wing, low and steady, until late into the morning, and when Priya finally settled, we'd hear Susan in her kitchenette, probably pouring something stronger than coffee.

But there came a night that exceeded Susan's capacity to cope, a night that changed Priya's routine and much more besides. It left a mark you've seen yourself—everyone has who follows neuroscience news—though you never knew what caused it. Nobody ever knew that except Priya and Susan Stanley and Nathan and me.

Nathan and I were finishing our evening work around midnight when the girl called out from the residential wing. We heard Susan go to her, and we paused our discussion because we knew neither of us would concentrate until Susan got Priya settled again. But this night was different. Susan hadn't talked to the girl long when Priya cried out with a sound of profound grief, and after that we heard both of them weeping.

Shortly after, Susan emerged into the corridor and closed the door behind her. She looked disheveled and defeated, her professional demeanor completely stripped away, her hair loose around her shoulders and her eyes swollen from crying. Whatever emotional reserves she'd been maintaining hadn't helped.

She stood motionless for a while, then she looked up at the ceiling-mounted neural displays and said something I'm not likely to forget.

"Why couldn't you give the girl a break?" she said, not angry or anything but loud enough for us to hear through our open door. "You, up there—what's another brilliant mentor to You?"

Nathan and I looked at each other in the fluorescent light of our office.

"She's done it, Diego," Nathan said.

I knew what he meant and wished I didn't. Susan had finally told Priya the complete truth about what had happened at Bristol—whatever that truth was. The waiting was over.

That's why I was concerned about Priya when I came to the lab the next evening and found her studying the neural activity displays instead of watching the courtyard. It meant she'd stopped her vigil at the entrance. And the quiet way the girl spoke of reorganizing neural connections concerned me more, because it sounded genuinely delusional.

Not that you could blame her for losing touch with reality. It was challenging enough to be confined to a wheelchair without being able to move her legs at all. But to learn that whoever she'd been waiting for was never coming back...

I was reviewing my third data set when Nathan arrived with a large package under his arm. Nathan was completely sober, which surprised me, and he was energized from a shopping trip to Brookhaven, which surprised me more. It was when he opened his package, though, that I thought he'd lost his professional judgment.

"Books for Priya," Nathan said. "Susan and I agreed this morning that the girl needs a new intellectual focus now, and since she can't attend regular school, I'm going to tutor her here."

He went on to explain that Susan hadn't been able to state the complete truth directly the previous night. She'd softened it, told Priya only that the person she was waiting for had taken an assignment far away—a prestigious position at a research institute in Lincoln, Orvandor—one accepted before the Bristol incident occurred. Susan implied that the distance made return impossible rather than explaining the full circumstances. It was a half-truth. Priya still didn't understand everything, but her waiting was over because no one could be expected to return from such a remote assignment.

"We must give the girl another focus," Nathan said, shelving the books and pouring fresh coffee. "Priya has a remarkable capacity for concentration—most intellectually gifted children do—that could destroy her if it isn't redirected into productive channels."

I thought the girl had already broken down and said so.

"Reorganizing neural connections?" Nathan said when I told him. "Good God, Diego—"

Susan Stanley knocked just then, interrupting him. She came in and had coffee with us and discussed Nathan's plan for tutoring Priya at the Institute. But she couldn't tell us anything more about the girl's new fixation than we already knew. When she asked Priya why she stared at the neural displays like that, she'd say only that she wanted something to remember.

It was about nine o'clock when Susan went back to prepare dinner. Nathan and I abandoned our chess game and moved to the observation room to check some equipment. It was then that the first neural pattern shifted.

It shifted suddenly, the way any spontaneous reorganization does, and rippled across the display in a cascading wave of activity. I didn't pay much attention, but Nathan nearly dropped his coffee.

"Diego," he said, "that was Subject Twelve! The motor cortex just reorganized!"

I didn't see anything particularly significant about it and said so. You can observe dozens of minor reorganizations on any given day if you're monitoring enough subjects.

"Not minor reorganization, you fool," Nathan said. "Subject Twelve—the chronic paralysis case—just showed complete motor cortex reactivation, then stabilized!"

I paid attention then, partly because the pattern really had stabilized instead of reverting the way spontaneous activity usually does, partly because anything that excites Nathan Hamilton that much deserves consideration.

We monitored the displays like two researchers at a critical experiment, but nothing else changed. After a while another subject's scan showed activity, though, and later in the night a whole series of them displayed reorganization patterns, forming a sequence that didn't make sense to us. They stopped changing around midnight and we returned to our office, but neither of us could focus on work.

"Perhaps we ought to find another research focus ourselves instead of developing one for Priya," Nathan said. He meant it as a joke but it sounded uncertain. "Something besides staring at neural scans every night, for instance."

"You think we're experiencing shared delusions from too much caffeine?" I asked.

Nathan laughed at that, sounding more like himself. "No, Diego. No two people ever had simultaneous and identical hallucinations of objective data."

"Look," I said. "I know this sounds irrational, but maybe Priya—"

Nathan wasn't amused anymore. "Don't be absurd, Diego. If those patterns really reorganized, you can be certain of two things—Priya had nothing to do with it, and the research literature will explain everything tomorrow."

He was wrong on at least one count.

The neuroscience journals the next day were filled with urgent communications and breaking news, but none of them explained anything. The conference calls and emergency meetings involved every authority available, and research coordinators everywhere were struggling to understand. It just couldn't happen, they said.

Nathan and I reviewed the literature systematically that night, and I learned more about neural plasticity than I'd absorbed in years of study. Nathan, as I've mentioned, is a trained philosopher, and what he couldn't recall about neuroscience, the emergency publications quoted with extensive citations. They included interviews with researchers at major institutes—Harvard, Stanford, Johns Hopkins, and facilities across the globe—but nobody could explain why all those subjects would show spontaneous motor cortex reorganization simultaneously.

It disturbed me to learn that Subject Twelve had been paralyzed for over three years following severe spinal trauma, that the case had been considered permanent and irreversible, that the motor neurons had been documented as non-functional but hadn't shown any activity until now. This particular subject—researchers referred to them by number for privacy—hadn't shown any change in associated regions, which puzzled the specialists considerably. I suggested to Nathan, only half joking, that maybe the associated regions hadn't reorganized because they weren't damaged enough to interest Priya's attention, but Nathan rebuked me sharply.

"Don't joke about Priya," he said sternly. "Regarding Subject Twelve—the neural pathways are so extensively damaged that signals need years to establish new routes. That means any reorganization would have started when Priya was only ten years old. Neural plasticity has well-established temporal constraints, Diego, and neuroscientists say they can't be violated."

"They said spontaneous reorganization across multiple subjects was impossible, too," I pointed out. "I'm not claiming that Priya really reorganized those neural pathways, Nathan, but if she did, she could have accelerated the timeline along with them, couldn't she?"

But Nathan wouldn't engage the argument. "I need air," he said.

I followed, but we didn't get farther than Priya's wheelchair.

There she sat, tense and absorbed, staring up at the neural activity displays. Nathan and I followed her gaze, the way you do automatically when someone ahead of you focuses intently on something. We looked up just in time to see more patterns begin reorganizing.

The first one to change was a subject with severe cognitive impairment whose scan suddenly showed activity spreading across the prefrontal cortex—rapid, like that—and stabilized at a level consistent with normal function.

Nathan said, "There went Subject Seven," and his voice sounded strained.

That was only the beginning. During the next hour, forty or fifty more subjects showed reorganization patterns, and their scans joined the group that had changed the night before. The sequence they formed still didn't resemble anything recognizable.

I left Nathan staring at the displays and went over to help Priya, who had finished for the night and was manually rolling her wheelchair toward the residential wing entrance, navigate the door. I assisted her inside where Nathan couldn't overhear, then I asked her how things were progressing.

"Slowly, Dr. Wolfe," she said. "I have approximately a hundred more to complete."

"Then you're really reorganizing those neural patterns up there?"

She looked surprised. "Yes, it's not particularly difficult once you understand the principles."

The odds were even that she was speaking metaphorically, but I proceeded anyway and asked another question.

"I can't discern any pattern in it, Priya," I said. "What are you creating up there?"

She gave me a very small smile.

"You'll know when I'm finished," she said.

I told Nathan about that after we'd returned to our office, but he said I shouldn't encourage the girl's magical thinking. "Priya's heard everyone discussing those neural reorganizations; the emergency meetings have been constant, so she's excited too. But she has far more imagination than most people because she's intellectually gifted, and she could develop a delusional system because she's traumatized. The thing to do is provide her with a rational explanation instead of validating her fantasy as reality."

Nathan was taking all this so seriously—because it was undermining theories he'd accepted as foundational all his professional life, like those neuroscientists who were panicking worldwide. I didn't realize how disturbed Nathan really was, though, until he woke me around 4:00 a.m.

"I can't sleep for thinking about those neural patterns," he said, sitting at my desk. "Diego, I'm frightened."

That from Nathan was something I'd never expected to hear. It startled me alert enough to sit up and listen while he articulated his concerns.

"I'm afraid," Nathan said, "because what is happening in those scans isn't consistent with established neuroscience. It just can't be, yet it is."

It was so quiet when he paused that I could hear the ventilation system humming. Finally Nathan said, "Diego, the human nervous system is as delicately balanced as any complex system. If that balance is disrupted too extensively, our understanding of consciousness itself will be fundamentally challenged."

Ordinarily I wouldn't have argued with Nathan on his own ground, but I could see he was constructing a mental scenario of all neuroscience collapsing like a house of cards, and I was afraid to let him continue.

"The problem with you philosophers," I said, "is that you think your experts have everything figured out, that there's nothing in the world their theories can't explain. Well, I'm a pragmatic researcher, but I know that your neuroscientists can measure brain activity until they're exhausted and they'll never learn who designed those brains in the first place. So how do they know that whatever designed them won't reorganize them again? I've always heard that if a person had sufficient belief, they could accomplish impossible things. Well, if a person has the focus that Priya's demonstrated, maybe she could reorganize neural pathways, too."

Nathan sat quiet for a moment.

"'There are more things in heaven and earth...'" he began, then laughed. "A quotation worn threadbare by centuries of repetition but as relevant tonight as ever, Diego. Do you really believe Priya is reorganizing those neural patterns?"

"Why not?" I responded. "It's as valid an explanation as any the experts have proposed."

Nathan stood and returned to his couch. "Perhaps you're right. We'll discover more tomorrow."

And we did. Nathan did, rather, while I was occupied running controlled experiments all day.

I returned to the lab slightly earlier than usual that evening, just before the day shift ended. Priya was sitting as usual alone in her wheelchair. In the dimming light I could see a stack of books on the floor beside her, books Nathan had given her to study. What stopped me was that Priya was staring at her legs as if they were the first ones she'd ever really seen, and she had that same expression of intense concentration I'd observed when she was studying the neural displays.

I didn't know what to say to her, thinking perhaps I shouldn't mention the neural patterns. But Priya spoke first.

"Dr. Wolfe," she said, without taking her eyes off her knees, "did you know that Dr. Hamilton is an exceptionally wise person?"

I said I'd always thought so, but why?

"Dr. Hamilton said this morning that I shouldn't reorganize any more neural patterns," the girl said. "He says I should concentrate instead on learning to walk again so I can travel and continue my studies with other researchers who share similar interests in consciousness and neural plasticity."

For a moment I was angry enough to confront Nathan if he'd been available. Anyone who would manipulate a disabled, vulnerable child like that...

"Dr. Hamilton says that if I can do what I've been doing to those neural scans, then it ought to be straightforward to reorganize my own neural pathways," Priya said. "And he's correct, Dr. Wolfe. So I'm not going to reorganize any more patterns in the database. I'm going to reorganize my own."

She looked up at me with her small, serious smile. "It took me a whole day to learn how to reorganize that first subject's motor cortex, Dr. Wolfe, but I could do this after only a few hours. Look..."

And she moved both her feet.

It's unfortunate that events in reality don't unfold like they do in fiction, because a compelling narrative could be constructed from Priya Stanley's capacity for reorganizing neural patterns through focused attention. In a story, Priya might have revolutionized neuroscience or destroyed the field entirely, depending on which outcome would engage the most readers and earn the writer the largest advance, but of course it didn't actually conclude either way. It ended in what Nathan Hamilton called an anticlimax, leaving everyone satisfied enough except a few neuroscientists who appreciate mysteries anyway or they wouldn't be neuroscientists in the first place.

The neural patterns that had been reorganized remained stable, but the sequence Priya had started was never completed. That unfinished sequence won't ever disappear, in case you've wondered about it—it's there in the research database where you can access it with proper clearance—but it will never be finished because Priya Stanley lost interest in it when she learned to walk again.

Walking was a gradual process with Priya at first because her legs had atrophied significantly—severe muscle wasting, Nathan said—and it took time to rebuild them. But within a few weeks she was moving around with crutches, and after that she never approached her wheelchair again.

Susan enrolled her in the Dalebrook school system, and before the academic year ended she was participating in adaptive sports and joining other students for social activities on weekends.

School opened up an entirely new world to Priya, and she adapted to the routine as smoothly as if she'd been doing it all her life. She learned extensively there and she forgot much that she'd learned independently through isolation. Before we realized what was happening, she was just like any other twelve-year-old, full of curiosity and energy, with no more ability to reorganize neural patterns through concentration than anyone else had.

I think she actually forgot about those neural scans along with other things that had meant so much to her when she was confined to her wheelchair and couldn't do anything but wait and think.

For instance, a young researcher named Jose Baker joined the Institute staff and began mentoring Priya in basic neuroscience. She attended his lectures and assisted with his experiments and called him Professor Baker, and after that she never mentioned traveling to find researchers who shared the interests of her former mentor. It was only natural, of course, because adolescents—healthy adolescents—move forward quickly. It's a sort of developmental necessity, Nathan says, against the traumas of existence.

When the academic year ended, Susan accepted a position at the Brookhaven facility where Priya could attend a specialized school for gifted students instead of the standard curriculum. When they transferred, the Dalebrook Institute felt so empty and purposeless that Nathan and I relocated and went to the Bristol research center for the consciousness studies program. We never heard from Susan and Priya again.

We've moved several times since; we're at a facility in Belvoria currently, working with the artificial intelligence research group. But everywhere we go, we're reminded of them. Every time we access the neural plasticity database, we see what Nathan calls the Priya Stanley Neural Monument, which is nothing but an unusual sequence sketched out with a hundred or so reorganized patterns of various types and magnitudes.

The structure of it is so incomplete that you'd never determine what it's supposed to represent unless you knew already what you were looking for. To us, the outline of a human brain is fairly clear. If you know enough to fill in the gaps, you can see it was meant to be a detailed neural map with only one region missing.

Nathan says that transient researchers like him and me forget old associations as quickly as adolescents do—and for the same adaptive reasons—so I'm not particularly interested now in where Susan and Priya Stanley are or how they're progressing. But there's one thing I'll always wonder about, now that there's no way of ever knowing for certain.

I wish I'd asked Priya or Susan, before they transferred away, which brain region she decided to leave incomplete.

---

It was only much later, after we'd settled at Bristol ourselves, that I learned the full story from one of the older technicians who remembered the accident. He'd been there that day, had seen the equipment malfunction that killed Dr. Stella Santos in the consciousness research wing. The same wing where Priya's mother had once brought her prodigy daughter for intensive mentorship sessions. The same wing that now stood renovated and renamed, as if new paint could cover old tragedies.

"The Stanley girl took it hard," the technician told me over drinks one evening. "Used to come here every week before her own accident. Dr. Santos was the only one who could keep up with that kid's mind."

I thought of Priya at her window post, asking Leonardo about Bristol news, watching every face that entered the courtyard. Nathan had always deflected my questions about exactly who she'd been waiting for, perhaps because he understood better than I did how grief could crystallize into something harder than acceptance.

"Did anyone tell her?" I asked. "About Dr. Santos?"

The technician shrugged. "Her mother said she would, eventually. But you know how it is with kids. Sometimes it's easier to let them hope."
problem_data.question: Who was Priya waiting for outside of the neural interface lab?
